According to the document context [p. 1], the Knowledge Store (KS) has four components:

(i) Knowledge Graph (KB): initialized with base KB triples and gets updated over time with acquired knowledge.
(ii) Relation-Entity Matrix: a sparse matrix, with rows as relations and columns as entity-pairs, used by the prediction model.
(iii) Task Experience Store: stores the predictive performance of LiLi on past learned tasks in terms of Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC).
(iv) Incomplete Feature DB: stores the frequency of an incomplete path in the form of a tuple.

These components are part of the Knowledge Store (KS), which is used for knowledge retention and helps future learning.

1. Direct name calling: Using animal names as insults (e.g., كلب> “dog”, حمار> “donkey”), mental ability insults (e.g., غبي> “stupid”, عبيط> “idiot”).
2. Immoral behavior: Associating negative moral traits or behaviors with the insult (e.g., حقير> “vile”, خاين> “traitor”, منافق> “hypocrite”).
3. Indirect speech: Using sarcasm, questions, and indirect language to convey offense (e.g., أذكى إخواتك> “smartest one of your siblings”, فيلسوف الحمير> “the donkeys' philosopher”).
4. Name alteration: Changing letters or sounds in a person's name to create an insult that rhymes with the original name (e.g., الجزيرة> “Aljazeera” to الخنزيرة> “the pig”).
5. Sexually related language: Using expressions that are derogatory towards certain groups or behaviors (e.g., خول> “gay”, وسخة> “prostitute”, عرص> “pimp”).
6. Simile and metaphor: Comparing a person to an animal, a person with a disability, or the opposite gender in a way that is degrading or insulting.
7. Societal stratification: Using insults associated with certain jobs (e.g., بواب> “doorman”, خادم> “servant”) or societal components (e.g., بدوي> “bedouin”, فلاح> “farmer”).
8. Wishing evil: Expressing a desire for harm or death to befall someone (e.g., ربنا ياخدك> “May God take (kill) you”, الله يلعنك> “may Allah/God curse you”).

These characteristics suggest that Arabic speakers use a range of linguistic and cultural references to express offense, often drawing on societal norms, cultural values, and historical contexts.

According to [p. 4], a bifocal attention mechanism is used to capture human behavior when generating natural language descriptions from infoboxes. It computes an attention over fields at a macro level and over values at a micro level, allowing the model to decide which field to mention next and then which value within that field needs to be mentioned next.

In more detail, [p. 5] explains that this mechanism is used because humans keep track of information at two levels: macro (deciding which field to attend to) and micro (deciding which values to attend to). The bifocal attention mechanism enables the model to do the same by computing separate attentions for fields and values, and then fusing these weights.

It's worth noting that this concept is not entirely new, as [p. 6] mentions that two-level attention mechanisms have been used in other contexts (unstructured data), where one needs to pay attention to sentences at a macro level and words within those sentences at a micro level.
